title: a collection of games i've prototyped using only vibecoding + Unity 6 in the past year and a half
author: Ok-Construction6173
selftext: here's a short video showcasing what can done when you can't write a line of code (i do have blender skills however) this isn't even showing half the games i've prototyped using AI like Codex and Cursor. some of these games have AI textures, some even have multiplayer. but ALL of the coding was done with Cursor.

replies.author: cdgalvan
replies.body: Can you elaborate a bit more on the gen AI texturing? Did you make UV maps and upload them to the model, which texted and gave them back? What was your process for getting textures that worked on the models, and how did you go about applying them?

replies.author: Ok-Construction6173
replies.body:
Ok ngl dude texturing still isn't a workflow that AI does well yet. Using Blender, I often have to use projection texturing and it looks messy as hell without some cleanup + retro styled pixelated graphics covering up the mess. You can use literally any model for textures. I used ChatGPT and Gemini usually. 

AI still probably won't understand what your UV map is if you tried that honestly lmao. One thing you CAN do is feed the AI a UV mapped face image for example, and ask it to change the face or features, and then use regular unwrapping in your 3D software. Texturing is still something I haven't been able to do that well yet, which is why you see a lot of untextured stuff here.

replies.author: Ok-Construction6173
replies.body:
It's a slower approach. It's also not a solution where "AI does everything". You still need a decent understanding of how Unity works. I switch between Codex inside of Cursor and Cursors default agents, Codex has been pretty good lately.   
  
I usually start by setting up a new project in Unity 6, making a new git repository using the local path of the Unity project (optional but recommended in case you screw up and wanna go back). I use Github desktop because it's simpler. Next I start by opening Cursor, File > Open folder > the root folder of your new Unity project, and then Cursor usually has everything it needs to work with from there. Then you can ask Codex or Cursor what the next best steps are for prototyping your game. I usually start with a player controller personally. Usually everytime the agent finishes it's job it'll tell you what to hook up in the scene step by step. Everything else is up to you, use Unity store assets (I recommend Animancer Pro for 3D animations because Cursor uses it very well) , make your own graphics, learn Blender like me, etc. From here on you'll be working with Cursor to troubleshoot any bugs, and keep adding stuff, try to keep everything modular, use data driven workflows when you can. 

It's still a bit of learning, trial and error but it's the best way to make a real indie game without coding at all. If you ask Cursor to do absolutely everything you'll end up with one of those incremental browser games you see everywhere on this sub :P

I will often ask the agent to help me code an inventory and it will usually give me a first pass and tells me what needs to be setup in the scene. This usually involves setting up panels and images on the canvas, TMP elements for text, and always item data.
